problem: 3D vision-language models ground objects only in static, fully pre-reconstructed scenes (meshes, point clouds) and cannot actively explore. End-to-end RL navigators can explore, but they are sample-inefficient, generalize poorly from limited data, and lack an explicit spatial representation. No single model both explores and grounds language or image goals online from raw RGB-D.
motivation: Real embodied agents work in partially observed scenes. They must repeatedly decide whether to commit to an object they have already seen or go look somewhere new, and they need memory that persists across many goals (lifelong navigation). The authors observe that grounding and frontier exploration can be posed as the same selection problem over a set of queries. That formulation lets 3D-VL pre-training and large-scale trajectory data (simulated plus real RGB-D) directly train exploration.
key_idea: Represent observed objects (online object queries in a dynamic spatial memory) and unexplored frontiers (frontier queries) as one candidate set. A language/image-conditioned spatial reasoning transformer scores all candidates and picks the argmax, which either grounds the goal object or navigates to a frontier. The model is trained end-to-end with Vision-Language-Exploration pre-training on over 1M trajectories.
insight: Casting 'where to go next' as grounding over a joint set of object and frontier queries lets semantic 3D-VL training guide exploration. Semantic frontier choice beats nearest-frontier exploration (Fig. 4c, at explore step 6: SR 50.0 vs 33.3, SPL 35.3 vs 30.3). Persistent query memory is what drives the lifelong GOAT-Bench gains: resetting memory per sub-episode cuts SR from 52.6 to 10.5 (object goals), 71.4 to 28.6 (description) and 60.0 to 26.7 (image). VLE pre-training gives consistent SR gains (OVON 27.8→33.3, GOAT 22.2→36.1, SG3D 22.9→27.9). The weak spot is path efficiency on short episodes: HM3D-OVON val-unseen SPL is 12.1 vs 19.8 for Uni-NaVid. This suggests that stop-and-reason frontier hopping with spins costs path length compared with video policies that head straight for a recognized target.
method: 2D/3D encoding: FastSAM segments each RGB frame into M regions. DINO pixel features are pooled per segment. The depth map is lifted with the pose into a world-frame point cloud (N points), encoded by a sparse-conv U-Net, and segment-pooled, giving segment-level 2D and 3D features.

Local query proposal: an MLP fuses the 2D and 3D segment features into initial queries. These are refined by PQ3D-style decoder layers (masked cross-attention to the features, spatial self-attention, FFN+Norm). Each local query holds a global-frame 3D box, a segment mask, a decoder feature f, an open-vocabulary embedding v and a confidence score s.

Dynamic spatial memory bank: local queries are matched to previous global queries by axis-aligned 3D box IoU, with low-IoU entries masked by a threshold. Matched pairs are fused by a count-weighted running average (n/(n+1), 1/(n+1)) over box, feature, vocab embedding and score; masks are merged by union. Unmatched queries become new entries, giving lifelong object memory without offline reconstruction.

Frontier queries: an occupancy map (occupied/free/unknown) is maintained. Frontier points on the known/unknown boundary become 3D coordinate queries, encoded by a 2-layer MLP and recomputed each time a target position is reached.

Unified grounding & exploration: a spatial reasoning transformer takes the concatenated object queries (f, v) and frontier queries, with type embeddings. It cross-attends to observation features and to the goal (CLIP text encoder for language/category, CLIP image encoder for image goals), then applies spatial self-attention. It outputs one score per candidate; the argmax either grounds an object or selects a frontier. The Habitat-Sim shortest-path planner then moves the agent, reasoning is re-run on arrival, and 18 frames are subsampled between consecutive targets.

Trajectory data: grounding trajectories come from ScanNet RGB-D videos paired with ScanRefer, ScanQA, Multi3DRefer, Nr3D and SG3D-VG, plus SceneVerse/SG3D on HM3D. Exploration trajectories are collected in HM3D via Habitat for OVON (290k), GOAT (680k) and SG3D-Nav (2k). Collection mixes random, optimal and hybrid frontier selection to avoid overfitting to the optimal frontier (Algorithm 1), and keeps a visited-frontier list.

Three-stage VLE training: Stage 1 trains perception with box IoU + mask BCE + vocab cosine + score BCE (50 epochs), after which query proposal is frozen. Stage 2 is VLE pre-training of the decision model with BCE on the unified scores over more than 1M trajectories (10 epochs). Stage 3 is task-specific fine-tuning with the same objective (10 epochs). Training takes about 164 GPU-hours on 4×A100.

setting.backbone: MTU3D: DINO (2D) + sparse-conv U-Net (3D) + FastSAM segments + PQ3D-style query decoder + spatial reasoning transformer with CLIP text/image goal encoders (trained); for A-EQA, GPT-4V / GPT-4o (frozen) answer questions from MTU3D-collected video
setting.training_data: Stage 1: ScanNet + HM3D RGB-D trajectories with instance segmentation labels. Stage 2: over 1M trajectories: 3D grounding/QA data (ScanRefer 37k, ScanQA 30k, Multi3DRefer 44k, SG3D-VG-HM3D 30k, SG3D-VG-ScanNet 13k, Nr3D 30k, SceneVerse-HM3D 48k goals) plus simulated HM3D exploration trajectories (HM3D-OVON 290k, GOAT-Bench 680k, SG3D-Nav 2k) with mixed random/optimal frontier strategies. Stage 3: task-specific navigation fine-tuning.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (360×640) + camera pose, Stretch embodiment
setting.action_space: high-level choice of an object query or frontier waypoint, executed by the Habitat-Sim shortest-path planner as low-level MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN_LEFT / TURN_RIGHT / LOOK_UP / LOOK_DOWN
setting.privileged: Ground-truth camera pose from the simulator. Motion to selected targets uses the Habitat-Sim shortest-path planner, i.e. the simulator navmesh.

numbers_note: HM3D-OVON (360 random episodes) and GOAT-Bench (90 random tasks) are evaluated on random subsets; baseline numbers appear to come from prior papers on full splits, so they are not strictly comparable. The 'Val Seen Synonyms' split is recorded as split 'val' with a note. The SG3D-Nav split and the A-EQA question count are not stated. OpenEQA has no val/test split, so 'test' is a placeholder. Ablations (VLE pre-training, spatial memory, exploration efficiency) appear only in Fig. 4 bar/line plots with printed values; the Fig. 4 caption swaps the (b)/(c) descriptions. The headline gains in the abstract and intro (+13.7 SR on OVON, +23.0 on GOAT) are measured against the best baseline on Val Seen; on OVON Val Unseen the SR gain over Uni-NaVid is only 1.3 and SPL is lower.
results: On HM3D-OVON, MTU3D reaches the best SR on all splits (Val Seen 55.0, Synonyms 45.0, Val Unseen 40.8 vs Uni-NaVid 41.3/43.9/39.5). Its SPL, however, trails on Synonyms and Val Unseen (12.1 vs 19.8 for Uni-NaVid and 19.9 for DAgRL+OD on Val Unseen). On GOAT-Bench it far exceeds modular and RL baselines (Val Unseen SR 47.2 / SPL 27.7 vs TANGO 32.1/16.5 and SenseAct-NN Skill Chain 29.5/11.3). On SG3D-Nav it gets s-SR 23.8 / t-SR 8.0 / SPL 16.5 vs Embodied VideoAgent 14.7/3.8/10.2. As an explorer for A-EQA it lifts GPT-4V from 41.8/7.5 to 44.2/37.0 LLM-SR/LLM-SPL, and 51.1/42.6 with GPT-4o. The 266M-parameter model runs at 3.4 FPS and was demoed without fine-tuning on a real robot (Jetson Orin + Kinect) in three scenes.
limitations: HM3D-OVON and GOAT-Bench are evaluated on small random subsets (360 episodes / 90 tasks), while baselines are presumably reported on full splits, which weakens the SOTA claims. Headline gains are quoted on Val Seen.
Path efficiency is weak on short open-vocabulary episodes (OVON Val Unseen SPL 12.1, below several baselines). Absolute performance on SG3D is low (t-SR 8.0).
Relies on ground-truth pose and the Habitat-Sim shortest-path planner (navmesh) to reach selected targets. Real-world evaluation is qualitative only (three scenes, no metrics).
